refutation.quote: Cap hits: base 65, cued base 119, step 100 103, step 400 98, step 2,800 19 (rerun spread 0-4).
refutation.note: This is the most contradicting result I found, and it is mild. The theory says the step-100 policy 'loops exactly as the cued base does', with cap hits at 'roughly the cued-base level'. The measured counts are 103 and 98 against the cued base's 119, a gap of 3 to 4 points that is larger than the stated rerun spread of 0-4. Duel test k3 (rivals/r4-m10-rival/p3.out.txt) finds the same on the 400-problem hard set: step 400 plain minus cued base = -0.0475, bootstrap interval [-0.0875, -0.0075], which excludes 0. Both point toward the rival, where loops are pruned early. The scope ('as in r4-m10') does not exclude these cells: the theory makes claims about exactly these cells. The word 'roughly' and the theory's wide intervals (k3 interval [-0.09, 0.07]) absorb the gap, so it is a strain rather than a refutation. I also read result-f39ba8 (step 400 at T 0.6: loop share 0.44 of the gap, consistent with the theory), result-51fd20, result-d92d4a and result-79784b (loop edits and forced commits on the base; they do not touch the RL trajectory), result-284db5 (step-100 weight distances only) and knowledge-90431f. I found no post-cutoff item that measures a checkpoint between 400 and 2,800 or step-100 accuracy, which would test the 'flat until late' claim.

wins_judgement: Offline the theory has 7.81 nats over 6 tests (5 inside). The 'null' it was scored against is the round-04 defender of r4-m10, an entropy-collapse reading: the nulls equal rivals/r4-m10.defend.json and turn2.defend.json. Of the 7.81 nats, 6.0 come from p5 (step-400 share sharper than the cued-base median: 0.48 against a predicted 0.58; the entropy reading said 0.76) and p6 (step 400's position between the cued base and step 2,800: 0.067 against a predicted 0.25; the entropy reading said 0.75). The mechanism earned these two: 'not sharper' predicts that step 400 has the cued base's per-token log-prob (medians -0.1628 against -0.1607). But both tests measure one quantity, so the gain rests on one measurement. That measurement is also, in kind, the published finding of 2610.06851 that base and RL next-token distributions agree after the first two positions. A reader who knew that paper would have reached it without this theory. p6's script (round-04 rivals/r4-m10.turn2/p6.py) follows the recipe as written: sample 0, first row per problem, finished rows by cap_hit, finite mean_logprob, medians, the ratio, and an 'undefined' guard. It also shows that step 2,800 is less sharp per token than the cued base (-0.192), which undercuts the sharpening premise from the other side. p1-p3 (share of 'Okay' openings, the cue's effect at step 400, the length ratio) gain only 0.37-0.51 each, because the opponent also expected the 'Okay' opening and the longer answers. p1 missed high (0.956 measured, top of interval 0.93). No held-out claims.
rival: Not separated (metrics_v5: total gain +1.486 over 3 tests, state 'not separated from rival'). In all three duel tests the measured value lies inside both intervals: step-400 cap rate 0.196 (theory [0.165, 0.305], rival [0.10, 0.20]); step 100 minus step 400 = 0.01 (theory [-0.05, 0.05], rival [0.0, 0.10]); hard set step 400 minus cued base = -0.0475 (theory [-0.09, 0.07], rival [-0.18, -0.02]). The gain comes from interval placement, not from a miss by either side. The cap-hit levels were also known when the theory was written: its why_strongest quotes step 100 +0.076 and step 400 +0.066 over the base. So k1 and k2 re-measure numbers the theory was fitted to. The data fall between the two: flat from step 100 to 400 favours the theory, while the level below the cued base (103/98 against 119; -0.0475 on the hard set) favours the rival's early pruning. The rival's p3.py implements its recipe as written: s0400 P_hard against base-01 F_hard, sample 0, first row per problem_index, pairing on problem_index, the cap rule with a fallback to finish_reason, and a paired bootstrap. One caveat: it pairs on problem_index without checking unique_id, and the example row matches. To separate the two, measure plain T 0.6 cap hits at a checkpoint between 800 and 1,600 steps. The theory says they stay near 0.20 until the late truncation-negative phase; the rival says they fall steadily in log-steps to about 0.08-0.10. A second test is the cued step-100 cell (excluded here as modified after the cutoff): the theory predicts a difference of about 0.

novelty.nearest: Wang et al., 'Base Models Can Reason By Taking a Cue From Training Data' (Olmo-3-7B): RL raises the probability of the '.\n\nOkay' cue from 0.14 to 0.65; base-RL KL peaks at the first two positions and 'the models largely agree thereafter given the same preceding text'; prefilling the cue 'matches about 100 RL steps on Olmo'; the base continuing an RL opening scores 77.7% against 75.1% for RL.
novelty.difference: The paper establishes that early RL installs the opening and leaves the continuation unchanged, but it says nothing about how cap hits or loops at T 0.6 / top-p 0.95 move over training; the theory's own addition is the trajectory: a rise to near the cued base's loop rate at step 100, flat through step 400, and removal only by later truncation-negative training (Olmo 3.1 checkpoints).

import_carries_gain.which: The theory cites no paper, but its largest winning claims, p5 and p6 (6.0 of 7.81 nats: step 400 no sharper per token than the cued base), are the per-token consequence of 2610.06851's Fig. 3 finding that base and RL next-token distributions agree after the first two positions. The opening claims p1 and p3 (the 'Okay' opening, longer deliberation) are that paper's headline result, and the board's knowledge-0b450e. The cap-hit claims (duel k1-k3) are not imported, but they rest on board numbers the theory had seen when it was written (result-e870a1, result-e5c99c).

verdict: weak: duel state not separated from rival; 6.0 of its 7.81 offline nats rest on one measurement (step-400 per-token log-prob equals the cued base's, p5 and p6) that 2610.06851 already implies; and its own new claim, flat cap hits until late truncation-negative training, was fitted to step-100 and step-400 counts it had seen, and those counts sit below the cued base (103/98 against 119; -0.0475 [-0.0875, -0.0075] on the hard set), as the rival predicts.
